ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inhaled therapy delivers medication directly to the airways, improving control of asthma, COPD and acute bronchospasm while minimizing systemic side effects. In low‑resource hospitals, choice of device, drug class and monitoring are guided by availability and local disease patterns.

b: Rapid bronchodilation for acute symptoms
Long‑term anti‑inflammatory control
Reduced systemic exposure compared with oral drugs
sections.p: Inhaled therapy uses devices (metered‑dose inhaler, dry‑powder inhaler, nebuliser) to deposit drugs in the bronchial tree. It is first‑line for reversible airway obstruction and for maintenance of chronic airway disease.

b: Short‑acting β2‑agonists (SABA) – rescue, onset <5 min
Long‑acting β2‑agonists (LABA) – add‑on to inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) – anti‑inflammatory, prevent exacerbations
Anticholinergics (SAMA/LAMA) – useful in COPD and severe asthma
sections.p: Drug classes, device selection, technique, and local disease prevalence shape therapy.

b: In acute severe asthma, give SABA via nebuliser every 20 min, add ipratropium if no response
For chronic asthma, stepwise add ICS, then LABA, then LAMA based on control
sections.p: In East African hospitals asthma, COPD, and post‑TB airway disease are common. HIV‑related bronchitis and schistosomiasis‑associated pulmonary hypertension also present, often with limited spirometry.

b: MDI with spacer is preferred when a reliable power source for nebuliser is lacking
Never give LABA alone – risk of asthma‑related death
In COPD with frequent exacerbations, add LAMA before LABA
sections.p: Examiners test understanding of device choice, stepwise management, and pitfalls in low‑resource settings.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical signs (wheeze, use of accessory muscles, response to trial SABA) and simple tools like PEF.

t.b: Is airway obstruction present and how severe? – Low PEF indicates obstruction; >80 % predicted suggests mild disease
Excludes alternative diagnoses (pneumonia, TB) when wheeze is atypical – normal lungs support primary airway disease
Detects hypoxia needing supplemental O₂ – <92 % warrants O₂ therapy

b: Acute severe asthma: high‑flow O₂, nebulised SABA q5‑10 min, add ipratropium, consider IV steroids if no improvement
Chronic asthma: start low‑dose ICS; step up to LABA+ICS if control not achieved
COPD exacerbation: SABA + SAMA, oral steroids, antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected
Avoid oral β‑agonists when inhaled form works – higher systemic side effects
sections.p: Treat the cause, then provide bronchodilation, anti‑inflammatory therapy, and monitor response.

b: Upper airway obstruction (e.g., epiglottitis) – stridor, no wheeze, rapid deterioration
Cardiac asthma (pulmonary edema) – crackles, pink frothy sputum, responds to diuretics not bronchodilators
PEF may be normal in early asthma or in patients using a spacer incorrectly
Chest X‑ray can be normal in severe obstruction; clinical assessment remains paramount
